name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
title: Long-Term Digital Preservation
answer: Long-term digital preservation covers the practices and systems that keep digital material readable and usable across decades, well past the life of the hardware and software that created it. It applies to research data, publications, government records, and cultural collections, and it sits within research data and repositories because those institutions carry formal mandates to keep scholarly output available. The work spans file formats, storage media, metadata, and the organisational commitments that outlast any single technology. It is distinct from backup, which protects against loss over short horizons, and from archiving in the everyday sense of simply moving files aside.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Long-term digital preservation covers the practices and systems that keep digital material readable and usable across decades, well past the life of the hardware and software that created it. It applies to research data, publications, government records, and cultural collections, and it sits within research data and repositories because those institutions carry formal mandates to keep scholarly output available. The work spans file formats, storage media, metadata, and the organisational commitments that outlast any single technology. It is distinct from backup, which protects against loss over short horizons, and from archiving in the everyday sense of simply moving files aside.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Preservation runs on layered storage, typically replicated copies held in more than one location and on more than one type of media, with checksums that detect silent corruption over time. Repository software such as DSpace, Fedora, and Archivematica manages ingest, description, and access, while format registries like PRONOM record what each file type is and what tools can open it. Persistent identifiers, most often DOIs, give each object a stable address even when its host moves. The infrastructure also depends on people: a funded institution, a named custodian, and documented succession when a system is retired.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core methods are migration, which converts files to current formats before the old ones become unreadable, and emulation, which recreates the original environment so the file can be run as it was. Preservation planning starts with format risk assessment, then sets a review cycle so actions happen before failure rather than after. Fixity checking compares stored checksums against recomputed ones on a schedule, and metadata capture records provenance, rights, and the technical details needed to interpret the object later. Researchers are usually asked to deposit data in open, well documented formats and to describe it well enough that a future reader can understand it without them.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on who may copy, migrate, and serve the material, since migration is itself a reproduction and licences or copyright may not permit it. Deposit agreements, retention schedules, and take-down procedures set out what a repository will hold and for how long, and provenance records show every change made to an object and by whom. Certification schemes such as the CoreTrustSeal and ISO 16363 give external evidence that a repository meets agreed criteria. The site's own practice of linking to the original paper rather than to a search tool reflects the same principle, that the preserved source should remain the point of reference.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward automated format identification and risk scoring, so that large collections can be triaged without manual inspection of every file. Emulation services delivered through the browser are making obsolete environments easier to reach, and distributed and decentralised storage models are being tested as hedges against single-institution failure. There is growing attention to the energy and cost of keeping many replicas indefinitely, and to the question of what to keep when storage is not free. The hardest problem remains institutional rather than technical: ensuring that funding, staff, and governance survive long enough to carry out the plans that have been made.
